analysis.one_liner: Blocks the SEC from banning payment for order flow, the practice behind commission-free stock trading.
analysis.headline: The bill drew only a sponsor and two Republican cosponsors, never received a committee vote or floor action, and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would write payment for order flow into law as untouchable. That is the practice where a brokerage sends its customers' stock orders to wholesale market makers and gets paid for it, which is how apps like Robinhood can charge customers nothing to trade. The bill would give firms a legal safe harbor for taking this money and would prohibit the SEC, stock exchanges, and the self-regulator for brokers from ever issuing a rule that bans or limits it. It was introduced in October 2021, sent to the Senate Banking Committee, and never went anywhere.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the biggest winners would be the wholesale market makers that pay for order flow and the zero-commission retail brokerages that depend on it, since the bill would permanently lock in their revenue model and shield it from regulators. Retail investors would keep paying no commissions, at least on the surface.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Zero-commission brokerages and wholesale market makers

how_it_helps.text: Gives brokers and dealers a legal safe harbor so that simply receiving payment for order flow can never by itself be treated as unlawful under state or federal law.
Prohibits the SEC, national securities exchanges, and registered securities associations from issuing any rule that prohibits, limits, or directs the receipt or use of payment for order flow.
Supporters frame the result as preserving commission-free trading and investor freedom by keeping the practice that funds it legal.

analysis.who_pays: The cost would fall on the regulators' ability to act, and potentially on retail investors: critics, including SEC leadership at the time, argued that orders sold for payment can be executed at prices slightly worse than the best displayed price, a small spread on millions of tiny trades that adds up. The bill would have made that debate legally moot.
analysis.who_pays_short: Regulators' authority; retail investors via spreads

drawbacks.text: The bill would foreclose any SEC rule limiting or banning payment for order flow, even if the commission found the practice harmed investors, because it bars any rule that prohibits, limits, or directs the practice.

It would also shield the practice from any theory of liability under state or federal law where receiving payment for order flow is the sole basis of the claim, taking a tool away from both regulators and private plaintiffs.

An honest supporter would acknowledge the fairness question: the order flow that brokers sell to market makers can be filled at prices a hair worse than the national best bid or ask, and this bill removes the main regulatory lever for addressing that, while leaving the bill's general preservation of brokers' other duties as the only safeguard.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and visible: commission-free trading for millions of small investors depends on this revenue stream, and an outright ban could have pushed some brokerages back to charging per-trade fees. But the bill goes far beyond protecting free trading — it writes a permanent legal shield around the practice and strips the SEC, exchanges, and FINRA of the power to limit it, so if the practice turns out to cost investors more in hidden spreads than it saves in commissions, no regulator could ever do anything about it. Locking in a business model against all future review is a heavy price for a benefit that more targeted rules could also protect.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Patrick Toomey introduced the Investor Freedom Act of 2021 on October 28, 2021, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
Two Senate Republicans cosponsored the bill; no other senators joined.
The bill received no further action after its committee referral, and it expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the SEC kept full authority to regulate or restrict payment for order flow — which matters given that the SEC was actively studying the practice at the time — and wholesale market makers avoided a statutory safe harbor they would otherwise have gained. Zero-commission brokerages and market makers keep the status quo either way, so the practical loser is the bill's premise that Congress should tie regulators' hands.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Regulators kept their authority over the practice

for.name: Sen. Patrick Toomey
for.role: U.S. Senator from Pennsylvania; introduced the bill while the Banking Committee's ranking Republican
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Investor Freedom Act of 2021 and guided no further action before leaving the Senate in January 2023.

against.name: Sherrod Brown
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or committee vote on the bill, leaving it without action after referral.

against.name: SEC leadership under Chair Gary Gensler
against.what_they_did: Publicly sought tighter rules on payment for order flow during this period, putting the commission on the opposite side of the bill's goal.

sides.party_line_note: Only three senators were ever attached to the bill, all Republicans, and no vote was ever taken, so there was no record of how the chamber would have split.

industries.industry: Wholesale market makers (firms that pay for order flow)
industries.note: These firms buy retail customers' stock orders from brokerages and profit on the difference between the displayed price and the price at which they fill the order. The bill would lock in that revenue stream permanently and bar any regulator from limiting it, while ordinary investors absorb the spread on millions of small trades.

Brokerages like the app-based platforms use payment for order flow to offer customers zero commissions, so the bill protects their free-to-user business model. The trade-off is that the money funding those zero commissions comes from the prices customers' orders ultimately get filled at.

Exchanges had an interest in more retail orders trading on-exchange rather than being sold to wholesalers; by locking in payment for order flow, the bill keeps that volume out of their hands and preserves the wholesalers' channel instead.
